summary: A description of NETRJS, a program from the University of Utah for submitting jobs to the remote job service on the UCLA IBM 360/91 across the ARPANET. A user prepares a job file on the Utah TENEX system, and NETRJS sends it and lets the user watch its progress. Utah wrote it because large compute-bound jobs were slowing its own PDP-10.

plainLanguage.summary: NETRJS lets a user at Utah send a job to UCLA's Remote Job Service and retrieve its output later. The RFC explains the commands and limits involved in using the service.

questions: how did utah submit jobs to the ucla 360/91
how does remote job submission work
how did a user retrieve rjs output
subtitle: A program for submitting jobs to UCLA's Remote Job Service from Utah TENEX.

tldr.problem: Large compute-bound jobs were affecting response time for other University of Utah TENEX users.
tldr.mechanism: NETRJS sends a local job file to UCLA's RJS, lets the user check job status, and retrieves print or punch output when it is ready.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents the commands and operating procedures for this remote job program.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 325 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. It documents the NETRJS program and service procedures described in April 1972.

sections.title: Why NETRJS Was Written
sections.content:
Utah had very large compute-bound jobs running continuously, reducing response time for other TENEX users. The RFC says Utah began submitting jobs to UCLA's IBM 360/91 through the Remote Job Service (RJS) in February.

A user creates a job file under TENEX, asks NETRJS to send it to UCLA, monitors its progress and retrieves the output when RJS reports it is ready.
sections.plainLanguage: Long-running jobs could slow other work on Utah's computer. NETRJS sends those jobs to UCLA and lets the user collect the results later.

sections.title: Submitting and Retrieving Jobs
sections.content:
The command interpreter supports sending a named file, retrieving printer or punch output, checking job status, viewing system status, logging out, disconnecting and other commands. The command language is based on a TELNET command interpreter and accepts partially typed commands when they are recognizable.

The user can sign off after a job is accepted and return later for its output. UCLA RJS limits which operator connections may be open at once, so the user may need to request printer, reader or punch access as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The user sends a file, checks the job's status and asks for output when it is ready. Printer output and punched output are retrieved through separate choices.

sections.title: Files and Operating Limits
sections.content:
NETRJS keeps no built-in list of valid UCLA terminal IDs. That information is stored separately in a file called PWD.SAV, so the program can be used from a TENEX system that can access the ARPANET.

Files sent to UCLA are converted to card images, with a line limit of 80 characters for jobs going to OS/360. Retrieved output lines may be up to 255 characters. The RFC also describes the control character, tab stops, editing characters and command behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The program reads account information from a separate file rather than keeping it in its code. Sent job lines are limited to 80 characters, while received output can be longer.

sections.title: A Sample Session
sections.content:
The sample session shows a user running NETRJS, sending two files, checking RJS status and retrieving printer and punch output into local files. UCLA reports when the job is accepted and when output becomes available.

The sample also shows that a user signs off from RJS and then quits NETRJS after retrieving the results.
sections.plainLanguage: The example follows a job from submission through processing to retrieval. The user can leave the remote service and return when results are ready.
